What to say: File Articles of Organization (LLC-1, $70) or Articles of Incorporation (ARTS-GS, $100) online through bizfile. The entity name and EIN are required for the business registration, seller's permit, bank account, and all city permits.

What to say: Register online at sftreasurer.org within 30 days of starting business; the fee is tiered by gross receipts ($55 up to $100k for 2026–27). outcomes.original: Filing step: Obtain a California Seller's Permit from CDTFA and register as an employer with EDD if hiring employees. What to say: Register online at cdtfa.ca.gov for the seller's permit (free, usually issued the same day); it is required for selling food and drinks. Set up workers' compensation insurance from a licensed carrier or State Fund before the first employee starts.

outcomes.original: Filing step: Submit the mobile food facility health permit application to San Francisco DPH at least two months before the intended opening date, with vehicle drawings, photos, menu, and a signed commissary agreement. What to say: Apply through the DPH portal with the BAN, two sets of scaled drawings of the truck interior showing equipment and plumbing, exterior and interior photos, a menu describing food prep steps, and a commissary agreement signed by a DPH-permitted commissary. The application is routed to Planning as an interagency referral to confirm zoning approval, then to the Fire Department for vehicle inspection. The 2026–27 fees are $470 application plus $414 (low-risk) or $690 (high-risk) plan review. Schedule the vehicle inspection at least two weeks in advance once plans are approved; the permit is issued after the inspection passes.

outcomes.original: Filing step: Apply for a Public Works mobile food facility location permit for each street location where the truck will operate, starting at least four months before the intended opening date. What to say: File online at sfpublicworks.org for each address; the fee is $1,151+ per location with half due at application. Post a yellow notice at the site for 10 days, mail notice to all addresses within 75 feet, and submit proof of posting. After a 30-day public comment period, Public Works issues a 90-day tentative approval if no objections are filed; unresolved objections go to a public hearing. Final issuance requires the DPH mobile health permit, SFFD fire certificate, DMV registration, and $2M liability insurance naming the City. The catalog warns location permits are routinely appealed by nearby restaurants, so apply for 2–3 candidate locations at once. If operating on a private lot, go through Planning and DPH for a zoning review instead.

outcomes.original: Estimated time: 90 to 270 days. Estimated government cost: $2,600 to $8,500. Notes: The day range (90–270 days) is the time to obtain the mobile food facility health permit and one Public Works location permit when both are granted, not a time to a denial or withdrawal. The health permit takes 30–90 days (catalog entry sf.mobile_food_facility_health_permit); the location permit takes 60–180 days including posting, neighbor notification, the 30-day comment period, and final issuance (catalog entry sf.mobile_food_facility_location_permit). These run sequentially because the location permit requires the health permit as a prerequisite, so the total is 90–270 days. The cost range ($2,600–$8,500) covers government fees only: entity formation ($70–$150, catalog ca.sos_entity_registration), business registration ($55–$700, sf.business_registration), FBN filing ($60–$120, sf.fictitious_business_name), food safety manager cert ($100–$250, ca.food_safety_manager_cert), mobile health permit ($880–$1,500, sf.mobile_food_facility_health_permit), and one location permit ($1,151–$5,000, sf.mobile_food_facility_location_permit). Each additional location adds $1,151–$5,000 and 60–180 days. These figures assume Planning confirms mobile food vending is permitted in C-2/Waterfront 2; if it is not, or if the concept must be changed to fit within a permitted use, no cost or timeline can be given until the zoning answer is known. The stall risk is high: the catalog warns location permits are routinely appealed by nearby restaurants, and the Fisherman's Wharf tourist corridor has 20 registered food businesses and 11 ABC licenses within 500 ft, so neighbor opposition and appeals are likely to push timelines to the upper end or beyond.
